passage: The pressure cooker whistles and two-year-old Nitin toddles straight toward the kitchen, eyes wide. His mother, Gopika, scoops him up before he reaches the stove and carries him to the window instead. A vegetable cart rattles past below. Nitin presses his palm on the cool grille, then pokes the fuzzy seed pod stuck in it. "Again?" he says, and Gopika tells the cart story once more, this time with a cow in it.

qa.q: What does Nitin poke after touching the grille?
qa.a: He pokes the fuzzy seed pod stuck in the grille.

qa.q: What does Nitin's rush toward the whistling cooker suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He seems full of interest in the new sound; his wide eyes show curiosity, not fear.

qa.q: What choice did Gopika make when Nitin headed for the stove, and why did it work?
qa.a: She lifted him away from the danger and carried him to the window, so his curiosity still had something safe and new to explore.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika to care for a child who heads toward every new sound?
qa.a: She has to stay watchful all the time, yet she also joins his interest by retelling the cart story with a cow added.

grounding: A toddler moves toward new sounds and textures and asks for a story again with a small change, while his mother keeps him safe.

passage:
"Papa, story!" Arohi pats the pillow.
"The crow and the pot?"
"Crow... blue!"
"A blue crow, then," Yogesh says. "The blue crow finds a pot..."
A scratchy sound starts outside the door. Arohi slides off the bed and heads for it.
"Wait, beta. That's Nani's broom. Hold my finger and we'll look together."
She holds his finger, crouches, and touches the stiff bristles. "Prickly!"
"Prickly. Back to the blue crow?"
Arohi climbs up again. "Pink crow."

qa.q: What colour does Arohi first want the crow to be?
qa.a: She says "Crow... blue!", so it becomes a blue crow.

qa.q: Why does Arohi slide off the bed when the scratchy sound starts?
qa.a: She wants to find out what the new sound is; for a moment the unfamiliar noise pulls her more than the story.

qa.q: What choice did Yogesh make when Arohi headed for the door?
qa.a: Instead of stopping her or letting her go alone, he offered his finger and went to look with her, so she could explore safely.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about telling the crow story with a new colour each time?
qa.a: He seems patient and playful, going along with every change; it may be tiring, but he keeps her interest alive.

grounding: A toddler asks for the same story with small changes and moves toward a strange sound and texture, with her father keeping her safe.

passage:
Note for Harsha's parents, Thursday
Today Harsha turned the reading corner into a ship bound for a moon made of idli. She gave every child a job: cook, captain, star-counter. At snack time she dipped her apple slice in her lemon rice "to see if it becomes a new fruit." She asked me why the moon doesn't fall. When one child called the ship game silly, her face dropped. I told the group that stories begin with ideas like hers, and we drew the ship a map. She brightened. Please keep asking her what she is building.
Usha, class teacher

qa.q: What did Harsha dip in her lemon rice?
qa.a: She dipped her apple slice in her lemon rice.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when another child called the ship game silly, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She seemed hurt, because her face dropped; she brightened again once Usha backed her idea.

qa.q: What choice did Usha make after the "silly" remark, and what did it change?
qa.a: Usha told the group that stories begin with ideas like Harsha's and drew a map with them, so the game went on instead of being shut down.

qa.q: What might the other children get out of Harsha's ship game?
qa.a: They each get a job and a story to step into, so the reading corner becomes an adventure for them too.

grounding: A child builds a make-believe world, asks why questions and tries odd food mixes, and needs an adult to protect her wondering from being called silly.

passage: In the courtyard behind the house, five-year-old Tushar crowned the calf king of the whole village with a marigold garland. "Why is the well water so cold? Why do crows hop? Why does the calf have no top teeth?" His sister Vidya, drawing water, laughed and answered what she could. When she suggested hopscotch again, like yesterday, Tushar groaned. "Same-same is boring." At lunch he stirred jaggery into his curd rice and called it royal food. Vidya almost said, "Don't be silly," and then stopped. "What does the king eat for sweet?" she asked. Tushar's eyes lit up.

qa.q: What did Tushar stir into his curd rice?
qa.a: He stirred jaggery into his curd rice.

qa.q: Why did Tushar groan at the idea of hopscotch?
qa.a: He felt bored at repeating yesterday's game and wanted something new, as "Same-same is boring" shows.

qa.q: What choice did Vidya make at lunch, and how did it help Tushar?
qa.a: She stopped herself from calling him silly and asked what the king eats for sweet, which let his make-believe keep growing.

qa.q: What might it be like for Vidya to have a brother who asks so many why questions?
qa.a: It can be a lot while she is busy drawing water, but she laughs, answers what she can and seems to enjoy joining his game.

grounding: A small child invents a pretend kingdom, asks many why questions and mixes foods, and his sister gives him room to wonder instead of calling him silly.

passage: Sit, Ojas, my boy. You think you are the first child in this family to fall into dinosaurs? When your Nani was ten, it was comets. I read one old library book until the spine cracked. I asked my Abba, "If a comet fell in the sea, would the fish get hot?" He had no idea, but he asked the science teacher for me. What I hated was copying the same multiplication table twenty times. Pointless, I thought, and I left it half done. Then my teacher said, "Nazia, comets move by numbers too." That stopped me. I finished the table that night. So, jaan, finish your tables, and then tell me about your T. rex.

qa.q: What did Nazia copy twenty times as a child?
qa.a: She copied the same multiplication table twenty times.

qa.q: Why did young Nazia leave the table half done?
qa.a: She felt the copying was pointless; her mind wanted comets and strange questions, not repetition.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Nazia treated the table?
qa.a: Her teacher linked numbers to comets, so the dull work suddenly connected to what she loved, and she finished it that night.

qa.q: How might Ojas take his Nani's story about her own tables?
qa.a: He may feel understood, since she also loved one topic and disliked copying, and he may be readier to finish his tables before the T. rex talk.

grounding: A grandmother remembers falling deep into comets as a child, asking odd what-if questions and resisting copying work that felt pointless.

passage: The lights went out at seven, with Simran's spelling list only half copied. By the glow of the emergency lamp she forgot the list and pulled out her battered space book instead. "Pema didi, if you fell into a black hole, would your feet stretch first?" Her cousin laughed. "Spellings first. The test is tomorrow." "But copying words ten times is pointless. I already know them." Pema held up the list. "Spell 'atmosphere'." Simran got it. "Spell 'gravity'." She got that too. "Fine," Pema said. "Say them aloud instead of copying, and we'll save the lamp for your black hole." The lamp flickered. Simran spelled faster.

qa.q: What did Simran pull out instead of the spelling list?
qa.a: She pulled out her battered space book instead.

qa.q: What does Simran's black-hole question show about what she wants?
qa.a: She wants to chase strange what-ifs; her pull toward space is much stronger than her interest in copying words.

qa.q: What choice did Pema make that got the spellings done?
qa.a: Pema tested Simran aloud instead of insisting on copying, and saved the lamp for the black hole as something to look forward to.

qa.q: What would change if Pema had simply scolded Simran for opening the space book?
qa.a: Simran might have felt her curiosity was a nuisance and dug in against the list; the quick spelling game kept both the work and her interest going.

grounding: During a power cut before a test, a child lost in space facts resists copying spellings that feel pointless, and her cousin finds a way through.

passage:
Last Diwali I refused to do the puja with everyone. I told Dadi I didn't see why lighting a lamp mattered if I wasn't sure I believed in it. I'd spent the week on old punk songs and a library book about Stoic philosophers, so I felt very grown up. My cousin Jatin, who loves a debate, told me to argue the other side, just for fun. So I did: the lamp as a way of saying the family is together, the ritual as a pause in a loud year. Halfway through, he grinned, because I'd started half-believing my own case. That annoyed me. I'd thought saying no was the same as thinking for myself. Now I think it was only saying no. This year I might light the lamp and keep asking my questions.
Alka

qa.q: What had Alka spent the week listening to?
qa.a: Alka had spent the week on old punk songs.

qa.q: Why was Alka annoyed halfway through the argument?
qa.a: Alka started half-believing the case for the lamp, which shook the idea that refusing was the same as thinking independently.

qa.q: What choice does Alka make about this year's Diwali?
qa.a: Alka plans to light the lamp and keep asking questions, joining in without giving up independent thought.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Alka refused the puja?
qa.a: Dadi may have felt hurt or worried that the family ritual was being rejected, even though Alka meant it as a question.

grounding: A teenager questions a family custom, tries new music and philosophy, argues both sides, and sees that refusing tradition is not the same as independence.

passage:
Debate club notes, Friday. Vandana, club mentor
Mehak, Class 10, argued for school uniforms in the first round and against them in the second, and was sharper both times. She grinned when nobody could tell which side she really held. Afterwards she played me a clip of throat singing she has just discovered and asked why our assembly songs never change. Then she said, a bit too proudly, that she had skipped her cousin's engagement "because traditions are for sheep." I asked which part she actually disliked, the ceremony or being told to go. She went quiet, then said, "Being told, I think." We agreed she will write next week's motion on choosing traditions rather than just refusing them. Her energy is a gift, and I want to keep giving it room.

qa.q: What did Mehak argue for in the first round?
qa.a: Mehak argued for school uniforms in the first round.

qa.q: What does Mehak's quiet pause after Vandana's question suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is rethinking; she sees that what she disliked was being told, not the engagement itself.

qa.q: What choice did Vandana make instead of lecturing Mehak about the engagement?
qa.a: Vandana asked what she really disliked and then offered her a debate motion, turning a proud remark into real thinking.

qa.q: How might Mehak's cousin see her skipping the engagement?
qa.a: The cousin may feel hurt or left out, taking it as a rejection of them rather than of a custom.

grounding: A teenager enjoys arguing both sides and new music, and a mentor helps her notice she has mixed up refusing tradition with being independent.

passage:
14 March, late
Tejas asked at dinner why we say grace when the farmers did all the work. Anita went still. I felt my neck get hot. My own father would have sent me from the table for that. I nearly said, "Because we do," and heard how thin it sounded before it left my mouth. So I asked him what he thought grace was for. He talked for ten minutes: gratitude, the farmers, whether God needs thanks at all. Some of it stung. Some of it was better than anything I could have said at fifteen. I am still unsettled tonight. But he kept talking, and he cleared the plates without being asked. Maybe tomorrow we will thank the farmers by name.
Francis

qa.q: What did Tejas ask at dinner?
qa.a: Tejas asked why we say grace when the farmers did all the work.

qa.q: How can you tell Francis felt unsettled by the question?
qa.a: Francis's neck got hot, the words "Because we do" nearly came out, and even late that night Francis writes of still being unsettled.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make at the key moment, and what followed?
qa.a: Francis asked Tejas what grace was for instead of shutting him down, and Tejas kept talking and even cleared the plates.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when his question was taken seriously?
qa.a: He probably felt respected rather than in trouble, which may be why he kept talking and helped clear up.

grounding: A parent is shaken when a curious teenager questions a family custom at dinner, feels both unease and pride, and listens first.

passage:
Late that night, Santosh texted his mother from his room.
Santosh: sorry if I was rude at dinner
Devika (Mum): You weren't rude. You asked why we touch the feet of relatives we barely know.
Devika (Mum): I didn't have a quick answer, and that rattled me a bit.
Santosh: so you're angry
Devika (Mum): No. Unsettled. And honestly a little proud. You think things through.
Santosh: I just don't get bowing to someone I met once
Devika (Mum): Tell me more. What would feel real to you instead?
Santosh: maybe saying namaste and actually talking to them?
Devika (Mum): Worth trying at Sunday lunch. And I'll tell you why Ammamma cares about it so much.
Santosh: ok. deal 🙂
Devika (Mum): Goodnight, beta.

qa.q: What did Santosh ask about at dinner?
qa.a: He asked why we touch the feet of relatives we barely know.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Devika describe about the dinner question?
qa.a: She felt unsettled and a little proud at once: rattled at having no quick answer, but glad he thinks things through.

qa.q: What choice did Devika make when Santosh asked if she was angry?
qa.a: She named her real feelings and asked what would feel real to him, which kept him talking and led to a plan for Sunday.

qa.q: What might it be like for Santosh to send that first message after dinner?
qa.a: He seems worried he crossed a line; finding his mother curious rather than angry lets him relax and agree to the plan.

grounding: A mother feels unsettled and proud when her son questions a family custom, and keeps the talk open by listening first.

passage: Every weekday at 7:40, Bao takes the same tram to the university in Melbourne, orders the same chicken rice from the same stall and sits at the same library desk. His flatmate Fatima teases him: "You've eaten that four hundred times." When the study group moved its meeting three times in one week, Bao felt his chest tighten each time the chat buzzed. On the fourth change he messaged, "Can we fix Thursdays at five and keep it?" The others agreed, a little relieved. By exam week, Bao's notes, rewritten carefully every Sunday, were the ones everyone borrowed. Fatima photocopied them too. "Fine," she said. "Your boring rice has a point."

qa.q: What does Bao order from the same stall?
qa.a: He orders the same chicken rice from the same stall.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling each time the chat buzzed with a new change?
qa.a: He felt uneasy; his chest tightened because the shifting plans kept breaking his steady routine.

qa.q: What choice did Bao make on the fourth change, and how did it go?
qa.a: He asked the group to fix Thursdays at five, and the others agreed, a little relieved themselves.

qa.q: How does Fatima's view of Bao's routine change by exam week?
qa.a: She starts by teasing him, but after photocopying his careful notes she admits his steady habits have real value.

grounding: A young adult likes fixed routines and familiar food, feels uneasy when plans keep shifting, and his steadiness turns out to be a strength.

passage: The notice board outside the hostel mess changed again on Monday: new dinner timings, a new rule about guests, a "surprise" menu. Lakshmi read it twice and felt her stomach knot. She liked her evenings fixed: dinner at eight, rasam and rice, notes, lights out by eleven. The student secretary, Anirban, shrugged as he pinned it up. "It keeps things interesting." "For you," she said. She went to the warden's office and asked, politely, whether the timings could stay the same for the whole term. The warden laughed but agreed to post a monthly chart. A week later, the warden asked Lakshmi to keep the mess attendance register, because hers was the only one with no gaps.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi like to eat at eight?
qa.a: She liked rasam and rice at eight.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi's stomach knot when she read the notice?
qa.a: The changes broke the fixed evening she relies on, so the shifting rules left her uneasy.

qa.q: What choice did Lakshmi make instead of just stewing over the notice?
qa.a: She went politely to the warden's office and asked for steady timings, which led to a monthly chart.

qa.q: How does the warden come to see Lakshmi's steady style?
qa.a: The warden sees it as reliability and trusts her with the attendance register, since hers was the only one with no gaps.

grounding: A young woman who prefers fixed routines and clear rules feels uneasy at constant changes, and her steadiness is valued as reliability.

passage: The small library above the Nandgaon post office had two keepers who could not agree. Ramesh Kaka wanted the old ledger, the same shelves and the same closing bell at six. Elizabeth, back from college, wanted a comic corner, floor cushions and a new layout every month. Each called the other's idea "nonsense" behind their back. Seema, twenty and on the evening shift, asked Ramesh Kaka what the ledger kept safe. "Every borrower's name for forty years. Nobody's book gets lost." She asked Elizabeth what the cushions were for. "The girls from the bus stand. They won't come in if it feels like an office." Seema set the ledger on the new counter and put the cushions beside the history shelf. Both keepers grumbled, and then both stayed late.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Kaka say the ledger kept safe?
qa.a: Every borrower's name for forty years, so nobody's book gets lost.

qa.q: Why did Seema ask each keeper what their idea was for?
qa.a: She wanted to understand what each preference protected instead of writing either one off as nonsense.

qa.q: Which choice did Seema make with the ledger and the cushions, and why did it work?
qa.a: She kept the ledger on the new counter and put cushions by the history shelf, so both the old trust and the new readers were served.

qa.q: How might the girls from the bus stand see the library after the change?
qa.a: They may find it less like an office and more welcoming, while their borrowing is still kept safe in the ledger.

grounding: A young woman sees value in both a traditional and a novelty-loving keeper by asking what each preference protects, instead of labelling either.

passage: "He's so dull," Dalia whispered, as Tomasz taped the paper cleaning rota back on the fridge for the third time. "And she's so flighty," Tomasz muttered later, when Dalia proposed a different cuisine for every Sunday dinner. Amara, twenty-one and sharing the Manchester flat with both, had nearly agreed with each of them. Instead, over tea, she asked Tomasz what the paper rota gave him. "Nobody argues about who did the bins. It's all there." She asked Dalia what the new dishes gave her. "Home was the same four meals for twenty years. This feels like breathing." That Sunday the rota stayed on the fridge, and the pot held Dalia's peanut stew. Tomasz took seconds.

qa.q: Where did Tomasz tape the cleaning rota?
qa.a: He taped the paper cleaning rota back on the fridge.

qa.q: What did Amara want to understand when she asked each flatmate a question?
qa.a: She wanted to know what each preference gave them, rather than settling for calling them "dull" or "flighty".

qa.q: What choice at the turning point let both flatmates' needs fit together?
qa.a: Amara let the paper rota stay while Dalia cooked something new, so order and novelty both had a place.

qa.q: What might Dalia feel when Tomasz takes seconds of her stew?
qa.a: She may feel accepted instead of judged as flighty, and see that he can enjoy something new when his order is respected.

grounding: A young woman refuses to label one flatmate dull and the other flighty and asks what each one's preference protects.

passage:
Pema has lived in four cities since I met her, and this year alone she's taken up pottery, Portuguese and a podcast about bridges. At our design firm in Pune, half the team loves her pitches. The other half rolls their eyes: "Another Pema idea, gone by Friday." I used to be in the second half. Then I watched her, in a client meeting, pull a solution out of something she'd learned in pottery class, and nobody else in that room could have made the leap. Still, her half-finished decks pile up. Last month I offered to be her "Friday person": she brings me one idea, and we write three next steps together. Two of them are already live.
Jomon

Shankar and I became friends the week he joined, eight months ago, from a startup in Kochi; before that, a bakery; before that, a year of teaching in Ladakh. In meetings he throws out three new ideas an hour. Some colleagues find it energising. One told me privately that he is "a flake who won't last the year." I don't agree with either extreme. His idea of reading circles at the bus depot is the best thing we have tried. But his project tracker has six rows marked "started" and none marked "done". passage:
Tuesday
Dear Diary, I packed my bag for tomorrow before dinner: maths book, geometry box, the signed permission slip. Then I checked it again. Ma'am picked me to collect the class notebooks because "Aditi never forgets." That felt nice. But in the maths test I wrote 7 × 8 = 54 and only saw it after I handed it in. I kept thinking about it all through lunch. After school Joseph asked me to play catch and I said no, because of homework. He looked disappointed. I finished everything by five and then just sat on the bed. I think I could have played for half an hour. Tomorrow maybe I will.

passage: In Farhan's house at the edge of the mustard fields, the school bag was packed every night before the lamp went out: slate, two notebooks, a pencil sharpened at both ends. His sister Alka laughed at him. "The school is ten minutes away." "What if the road floods?" he said. The teacher had made Farhan keeper of the library cupboard key, because he never lost anything. But on Saturday, when the boys shouted from the maidan for a cricket match, Farhan stayed on the charpai, rubbing out a letter he had written slightly crooked. Alka sat beside him. "The letter is fine. The match won't wait." He looked at the page, then at the field, and slowly closed the notebook.

qa.q: What was Farhan made keeper of?
qa.a: He was made keeper of the library cupboard key.

qa.q: What does rubbing out a slightly crooked letter suggest Farhan is worried about?
qa.a: He worries that even a tiny flaw makes his work wrong, so he keeps fixing it instead of going to play.

qa.q: What turning point came when Alka sat beside him?
qa.a: She told him the letter was fine and the match would not wait, and he chose to close the notebook.

qa.q: How does Alka see her brother's careful habits?

grounding: A village boy packs his bag each night and is trusted for never losing things, but his worry over small mistakes crowds out play.
